newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU delay would need treaty renegotiation - Hesse.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay would need treaty renegotiation - Hesse.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Helmut Hesse was quoted on Tuesday saying a delay to launching the European single currency would force the Maastricht Treaty to be renegotiated and ratified by European Union member states.

Hesse, in an interview with the Nordsee Zeitung newspaper, also said prestige-driven efforts of some countries to join the starting lineup of European economic and monetary union (EMU) did not mean that the Maastricht criteria could be ignored.
"At the moment, all member states are wildly determined to fulfill the criteria and be there at the start. It would be a loss of prestige to miss the start," he told the newspaper.
But he added, "we must insist the criteria are strictly observed because the entry of Germany is only allowable under the constitution if the currency union is stable."

Both the Bundesbank and Bonn have said they wanted Germany to hit the three-percent budget deficit-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio this year stipulated by Maastricht. But record post-war unemployment has pressured state finances and put reaching that goal into doubt.
Hesse, who is also president of the central bank of Bremen, Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, said it was possible that Germany could miss the planned start of EMU in 1999.
Outlining a possible scenario, Hesse noted that the Maastricht Treaty said countries could reapply to join a year after the EMU launch.

He also said legal experts believed it would be possible for smaller countries that meet the treaty's demands to agree to wait for larger countries to join. "However, this is not a forecast. It is a theory," he said.
If Maastricht has to be renegotiated, "everything will be new. Then, we cannot expect the conditions as they stand in the treaty now to be put in again," he added.
Hesse warned that failure to take the right decisions could put off European currency union for the next 20 years.
